/-!
# Conjecture 8.52

by A. Yu. Olshanskii

(Well-known problem). Do there exist infinite finitely presented periodic groups?

A group is *periodic* (or *torsion*) if every element has finite order. A group is
*finitely presented* if it is isomorphic to a quotient of a free group on finitely many
generators by the normal closure of finitely many relators, i.e. to
`PresentedGroup rels` for some finite set `rels` of elements of `FreeGroup (Fin n)`.
Since being infinite and being periodic are invariant under isomorphism, the question
can be stated directly for groups of the form `PresentedGroup rels`.

The notebook adds the cross-reference "Compare with 6.3".

*Reference:* [The Kourovka Notebook](https://arxiv.org/abs/1401.0300v46)
-/

blocks.docstring:
Do there exist infinite finitely presented periodic groups?

That is, do there exist $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and a finite set $R$ of elements of the free group
$F_n$ on $n$ generators such that the group
$\langle x_1, \dots, x_n \mid R \rangle = F_n / \langle\langle R \rangle\rangle$
is infinite and every element of it has finite order?

That is, do there exist $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and a finite set $R$ of elements of the free group

$\langle x_1, \dots, x_n \mid R \rangle = F_n / \langle\langle R \rangle\rangle$
is infinite and every element of it has finite order?

@[category research open, AMS 20]
theorem kourovka.«8.52» : answer(sorry) ↔
    ∃ (n : ℕ) (rels : Set (FreeGroup (Fin n))), rels.Finite ∧
      Infinite (PresentedGroup rels) ∧ Monoid.IsTorsion (PresentedGroup rels) := by
  sorry

claims.decomposer_note: Single yes/no existence question (Prop: ∃ a group that is infinite, finitely presented, and periodic/torsion, i.e. every element has finite order); 'finitely presented' has no Mathlib predicate for groups (only Group.FG exists) so it must be defined via a finite generating set and finite relator set, e.g. a PresentedGroup on a Fin n with finitely many relators; periodicity is Mathlib's Monoid.IsTorsion; the parenthetical '(Well-known problem)' and 'Compare with 6.3' are remarks/cross-references, not further questions.
claims.reviewer_why: All eight candidates state the same mathematically correct proposition: answer(sorry) ↔ ∃ n, ∃ finite rels ⊆ FreeGroup (Fin n), Infinite (PresentedGroup rels) ∧ Monoid.IsTorsion (PresentedGroup rels) (c02/c04/c08 phrase it as ∃ G isomorphic to such a PresentedGroup, which is equivalent since Infinite and IsTorsion are MulEquiv-invariant). 'Periodic' = Monoid.IsTorsion (∀ g, IsOfFinOrder g), 'finitely presented' = finitely many generators (Fin n) and a finite relator set, 'infinite' = Infinite. Boundary cases (n = 0 gives the trivial group; empty relators give a free group, which is torsion only if trivial) are excluded by Infinite, so the RHS genuinely constrains answer(sorry); answer(True) is the positive answer. c05 chosen because it uses the direct PresentedGroup encoding (no bespoke IsFinitelyPresented, which is generic mathematics and per CONTRIBUTING would belong in FormalConjecturesForMathlib rather than the problem file), has the fullest, accurate module and theorem docstrings (mentions the '(Well-known problem)' remark and the 6.3 cross-reference as remarks), follows Kourovka/ file style, and compiles with only the 'declaration uses sorry' warning.

import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Conjecture 8.52

by A. Yu. Olshanskii

(Well-known problem). Do there exist infinite finitely presented periodic groups?

A group is *periodic* (or *torsion*) if every element has finite order. A group is
*finitely presented* if it is isomorphic to a quotient of a free group on finitely many
generators by the normal closure of finitely many relators, i.e. to
`PresentedGroup rels` for some finite set `rels` of elements of `FreeGroup (Fin n)`.
Since being infinite and being periodic are invariant under isomorphism, the question
can be stated directly for groups of the form `PresentedGroup rels`.

The notebook adds the cross-reference "Compare with 6.3".

*Reference:* [The Kourovka Notebook](https://arxiv.org/abs/1401.0300v46)
-/

namespace Kourovka.«8.52»

/--
Do there exist infinite finitely presented periodic groups?

That is, do there exist $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and a finite set $R$ of elements of the free group
$F_n$ on $n$ generators such that the group
$\langle x_1, \dots, x_n \mid R \rangle = F_n / \langle\langle R \rangle\rangle$
is infinite and every element of it has finite order?
-/
@[category research open, AMS 20]
theorem kourovka.«8.52» : answer(sorry) ↔
    ∃ (n : ℕ) (rels : Set (FreeGroup (Fin n))), rels.Finite ∧
      Infinite (PresentedGroup rels) ∧ Monoid.IsTorsion (PresentedGroup rels) := by
  sorry

end Kourovka.«8.52»

items: Finitely presented is encoded as 'the group PresentedGroup rels for some n : ℕ and finite rels : Set (FreeGroup (Fin n))' rather than 'a group G isomorphic to such a PresentedGroup'; this is equivalent for this question because Infinite and Monoid.IsTorsion transfer along MulEquiv, and it avoids introducing a bespoke IsFinitelyPresented predicate.
Generators are indexed by Fin n (a finite type up to equivalence), relators by a Set with a Set.Finite hypothesis rather than a Finset with coercion.
Periodic is taken as Monoid.IsTorsion (every element has finite order), i.e. unbounded exponent is allowed, matching the standard meaning of 'periodic group' and the notes in the decomposition table.
The parenthetical '(Well-known problem)' and 'Compare with 6.3' are treated as remarks and only mentioned in the module docstring; the content of problem 6.3 is not asserted.

reviewer_notes: Single-slot problem; the decomposition is correct ('(Well-known problem)' and 'Compare with 6.3' are remarks, not further questions). No candidate omitted the slot and no omission reasons needed weighing. c01/c03/c05/c06 are textually near-identical statements; c07 uses Finset instead of Set.Finite; c02/c04/c08 quantify over an abstract G : Type isomorphic to a finite presentation — all equivalent. c04's `@[category test]` and c08's `@[category API]` lemma for the bespoke predicate are fine but unnecessary once the predicate is dropped. Final file is c05 verbatim; compiled with `lake env lean --json` — no errors, only the expected sorry warning. Reference URL uses v46 as given in the task's source citation (existing Kourovka files cite v40).
